chunks: "Every real passive has the other two elements hiding inside it, and they come from geometry and materials.
A resistor is a conductor, so it has some lead and trace inductance in series, and its two end caps and the body have a bit of capacitance across it, a fraction of a picofarad.
A capacitor has resistance in its plates and terminals, that's the ESR, and it has inductance from the current loop through the plates and leads, the ESL.
It also leaks a tiny bit of DC current through the dielectric.
An inductor has the resistance of the copper winding, that's DCR, and capacitance between adjacent turns that sits across the whole coil, plus a loss term from the core.
The result is that every part is only the ideal part over a band. A capacitor looks like a capacitor up to its self-resonant frequency, where its ESL cancels the capacitance.
Above that it's an inductor. An inductor does the opposite: it's an inductor up to its resonance, then a capacitor. For example a 100 nanofarads 0402 with about 0.
5 nanohenries of ESL resonates near 22 megahertz, so above that it's not decoupling anything the way you'd draw it.
So in practice I pick parts and package sizes by looking at the impedance curve, not the nominal value, and I keep the loop area small because mounting inductance often dominates the part's own ESL."
